posts.title: Is the Great Reset on the Horizon?
posts.excerpt: Three news pieces have really set my imagination on fire. First, a news piece which has been making the headlines :- S&P Global has assigned A+ ratings to bonds financing large AI infrastructure projects, even though the yields are hovering around 6.8% and several of these instruments are being treated by lenders as junk-risk in […]
posts.content:
Three news pieces have really set my imagination on fire. First, a news piece which has been making the headlines :-

S&P Global has assigned A+ ratings to bonds financing large AI infrastructure projects, even though the yields are hovering around 6.8% and several of these instruments are being treated by lenders as junk-risk in practice.

When did this exact combination of A+ ratings with Junk Grade Yields most famously happen ?

The Sub Prime Crisis of 2008 ~ The Great Meltdown.

The next news piece is even more ominous :-

Oracle’s OpenAI-linked data centre buildout is running into a financing wall. US banks have stepped back. Borrowing costs have doubled. Oracle has already burned through $58 billion of debt in just 2 months. (Report ~ https://lnkd.in/gGUH_CXG)

Now Oracle is demanding up to 40% upfront payments from new customers, and its considering selling Cerner.

In 2022, Cerner was acquired by Oracle for about $28.3 billion to anchor Oracle’s push into healthcare cloud and data-driven medicine.

The acquisition was framed as strategic, long-term, and defensive against Big Tech encroachment into healthcare.

But the scariest part is Oracle’s announcement of 30,000 job cuts to reallocate saved salary funds to keep the AI infrastructure engine running.

Brilliant !

Now the super-duper scary part is how India is tied up in this AI mad rush ~ private and public both; head, neck, spine everything:-

In October 2025, Adani’s announced a massive AI data centre push.
In January 2026, Ambani’s announced another hyperscale AI facility in Jamnagar.

Also, GOI in a major push has requested all the India IT companies to re-orient towards AI infrastructure, APP or service delivery models.

On 1 February 2026, yesterday the Indian Finance Minister in her budget speech categorically backed the AI data infrastructure and offered a tax holiday till 2047 for all foreign cloud companies.

The foreign companies will save on billions of tax and India becomes a lucrative Global Data Centre set-up country.

This may well be the single most consequential budget signal, far more than headline welfare, deficit financing numbers or SGB Tax rates.

However, the red beacon flashing is the US financing ebb for the AI data centres which is evident from the S&P A+ rated yet junk bond yield level returns.

In the 2008 sub-prime crisis, Indian stock markets just mirrored the US stock market without major banking or finance sector structural resets.

But this time, India is in deep partnership with the US AI Companies and will see a true blood-bath if a crisis occurs.

Just one solace for now, GOI has not announced any incentives for Indian Financial Institutions to back this major development. Hopefully the Asian Banks mentioned in the TOI news report are Japanese, Saudi or Chinese one’s.

Once bitten, twice shy !

posts.title: Childhood Stamps & Geo-Politics
posts.excerpt: Back home in Calcutta, while rummaging through an old cupboard, I stumbled upon my childhood stamp collection. A faded album. Yellowing pages. Small pieces of the world trapped under cellophane. These weren’t just stamps. They were my first exposure to global history. Some of these stamps were issued after the 1979 Iranian Revolution, when the […]
posts.content:
Back home in Calcutta, while rummaging through an old cupboard, I stumbled upon my childhood stamp collection.

A faded album. Yellowing pages. Small pieces of the world trapped under cellophane.

These weren’t just stamps. They were my first exposure to global history.

Some of these stamps were issued after the 1979 Iranian Revolution, when the Shah was overthrown and Ayatollah Khomeini came to power. In a single political rupture, Iran shifted from being the United States’ closest ally in the Middle East to its primary adversary.

There are a bunch of beautiful stamps from Hungary, some of them reproducing Renaissance-era paintings ~ Madonna & the child, saints, scholars and divinity rendered in oil centuries ago.

I have a stamp of 1967 Soviet Union, commemorating 50 years of the October Revolution. This was the apogee of Global Communist Power. Soviet Russia has already sent Sputnik the first artificial satellite to orbit, Yuri Gagarin has gone to space, Cuban missile crisis has already unfolded and Vietnam war in 1967 will see major escalation from the United States.

Interestingly, 2025 also marks the centenary of the Communist Party of India.

But my most intriguing stamps were from two pseudo-states:

Republic of Saharaui ~ This is a piece of land not universally recognized by the UN and is located along Africa’s west coast. This is a contested land, it is claimed by Morocco and designated as its south-western province.

This area is a part of the Western Sahara, a geologically old and fossil-rich. Over the last few decades, multiple dinosaur remains have been identified in Western Sahara, especially from the Late Cretaceous period.

Dinosaurs are perfect symbols to be used in stamps. They bypass politics and speak in geological time. These stamps narrate that this land existed long before Morocco, Spain, the UN or modern nation-states.

The second pseudo-state in this collection is the Republic of Buriatia. Located in Siberia and formally part of the Russian Federation, it is home to a mixed Russian–Mongolian population and is one of the few predominantly Buddhist regions within Russia.

These Buriatia stamps are products of the late 1990s, issued in the uncertain aftermath of the Soviet collapse. During the 1990s, several regions, autonomous republics, and pseudo-states issued visually striking stamps aimed primarily at international collectors, not domestic postal use.

Today, when I write about history and geo-politics, I realise these stamps were my first archive. Some childhood interests simply evolve.

posts.title: South Asia’s First Rapid Transport System
posts.excerpt: 53 years back, on December 29, 1972, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi laid the foundation stone for India’s first metro system ~ The Kolkata Metro. Exactly a year earlier India has won decisively against Pakistan and created Bangladesh. India has seen 10 million refugees coming in from Bangladesh. This was on top of 5 million refugees […]
posts.content:
53 years back, on December 29, 1972, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi laid the foundation stone for India’s first metro system ~ The Kolkata Metro. Exactly a year earlier India has won decisively against Pakistan and created Bangladesh. India has seen 10 million refugees coming in from Bangladesh. This was on top of 5 million refugees during partition at 1947.

It was a bold decision for its time. Construction began in 1973–74, when India was still grappling with post-war economic stress, and Bengal was creaking on its reams with a massive pressure on its food security and civil infrastructure. Kolkata Metro a fully underground rapid transit system finally opened to the public in 1984.

Interestingly 3 other Metro Projects also became operational around the same time and all 3 have fascinating tales to tell.

  1. Hong Kong was still under the British and have not yet been handed over to China. There was immense transport stress in Hong Kong which coupled with other civic issues led to wide spread riot in Hong Kong. As a response the British colonial government started the metro railway to ease transport stress in 1979.
  2. Communist North Korea firmly in Soviet Bloc during this time, planned a metro railway. It was a civil-defence and vanity project for the communists. This was the height of the Cold War and immediately US backed South Korea announced their own metro railway. Both went operational around ’73 – ’74.

The Kolkata Metro, which went on to become one of the city’s defining markers, also found a place in popular culture. It was featured in Mile Sur Mera Tumhara, Doordarshan’s iconic musical celebrating national unity and cultural diversity.

Born in a moment of national upheaval, the Kolkata Metro was not just a transport project, it was a statement that India would build for the future even when the present was under strain.

posts.title: The Christmas Day Plot
posts.excerpt: The viceroy’s seasonal lunch and ball was more than a party, it was the ritual heart of imperial India, a single glittering event where the whole machinery of colonial authority came to be seen, recognized and reinforced. On every 25th December afternoon and into the evening, the great drawing rooms and banquet halls were filled […]
posts.content:
The viceroy’s seasonal lunch and ball was more than a party, it was the ritual heart of imperial India, a single glittering event where the whole machinery of colonial authority came to be seen, recognized and reinforced.

On every 25th December afternoon and into the evening, the great drawing rooms and banquet halls were filled with the British elites in India.

Because the event assembled the empire’s top people in a single confined space, it created an unusual concentration of value and vulnerability.

In 1915 right amongst the raging World War 1, Bagha Jatin the legendary revolutionary planned to strike on the administration.

Bagh Jatin’s plan was to strike exactly when the British were distracted with Christmas celebration and the Viceroy’s event. He planned to converge on Calcutta then the capital of British Raj for more than 175 years. New Delhi was still 15 years away.

To achieve a paralysing effect, the plan combined targeted sabotage with mass mobilisation. Teams with gelignite and smuggled dynamite were assigned to key rail bridges and telegraph junctions leading into Calcutta. Their mission was to delay relief columns for as long as possible.

Simultaneously, armed guerrilla detachments, issued with rifles and instructed in basic fieldcraft, would emerge from the countryside and the city’s underbelly to seize police stations, attack intelligence outposts, and free political detainees from jail.

The objective was not to hold Calcutta in the classic sense but to throw the machine of colonial command into disorder long enough for sympathetic units within the Indian army and recruited mutineers to switch sides.

Bagha Jatin has already once orchestrated the 10th Jat uprising in 1910, which was the first time since 1857 Sepoy Mutiny that a British Indian Army Unit has ever rose up.

Bagh Jatin has already sent out feelers to engage with the Rajput troops then stationed at Fort William, Calcutta. With the top colonial leadership trapped in a city that they no longer controlled, it was hoped that a wider rebellion across Bengal Presidency would be triggered.

But the key to the guerilla uprising by Bagha Jatin was dependent on the smuggled arms supposed to be sent by the Germans through sea.

US Arms & Annie Larson

In early 1915 the plan moved beyond India’s shores, into the world of global arms dealers, shipping agents, and cloak-and-dagger diplomacy.

In New York City, the Krupp Agency arranged one of the largest arms purchases during the First World War. This Agency was operating under instructions from Franz von Papen, the ambitious military attaché of the German embassy in Washington and a master of covert operations. Franz Von Papen was instructed by Berlin to secure arms for the Indian revolutionaries against the British.

The arms order was staggering, at 30,000 rifles and 400 rounds of ammunition per rifle, it was enough to equip whole battalions, a force that could rival the smaller British garrisons in India.

Krupp Agency disguised the paperwork in false bills of lading. To ordinary port workers the crates looked like machine parts, agricultural equipment or canned goods. To the Germans and their Indian allies, they were the promise of a second 1857.

The cargo was loaded aboard the Annie Larsen, a modest schooner chartered for the task. Annie Larsen’s mission was as daring. She was to sail into the Pacific, rendezvous near the remote Socorro Island, and there transfer her cargo mid-sea to another vessel, the SS Maverick.

SS Maverick was a larger, more reliable ship flying a neutral flag, was then supposed to carry the arms across the Pacific, through Dutch-controlled waters in Southeast Asia, and finally into the Bay of Bengal.

From there, Bagha Jatin’s men would receive the cargo at Balasore or the Sundarbans and disperse it inland through a web of underground cells.

Annie Larsen reached the rendezvous point at the pre decided time and waited for SS Maverick. After waiting for 2 weeks amidst hostile waters finally Annie Larsen decided to turn back to America. Right after Annie Larsen turned back SS Maverick reached the rendezvous point. The planned arms transfer failed.

But why did this happen?

Behind this was the German Double Agent Vincent Kraft.

Vincent Kraft was a German planter who enlisted in the Imperial German Army at the beginning of World War I and fought in France. Kraft was involved in anti-German activities and faced court martial which could possibly lead to a death penalty.

Then a bizarre turn of events unfolded. Kraft was given an option by the Germans, to either face court martial or return to Jakarta (then a Dutch colony) and aid in coordinating arms shipments for the Indian revolutionary network.

Kraft returned to Jakarta and reported to the German Consul in China. Here he secretly established contact with the British embassy in Jakarta and showed his true colour. In Singapore on June 1915 Kraft passed on information about the arms shipment sent by the Germans to the British and a map with markings of the possible ship landing in the Orissa coast.

Immediately the British delayed SS Maverick in some pretext and parallelly started their hunt for Bagha Jatin and his network. This eventually led to the battle with Bagha Jatin’s guerilla army on the bank of Buribalam river and their martyrdom.

All through this Kraft agreed to fully cooperate with the British in exchange for a substantial sum of money. Kraft was promised safe emigration to the United States, away from European & Indian revolutionary vengeance.

Meanwhile Bagha Jatin’s remaining members started revenge killing of the British CID and within a year almost 20% of the officer cadre of CID was assassinated.

The British and Americans planned to bury Kraft’s old identity, and gave him a completely fabricated name and background so he could vanish into the immigrant tide of New York or Chicago.

40 years later, Kraft’s true identity was revealed when secret Indian government archives were opened to the public in 1950s after Independence. But the most intriguing part is that even a century later, papers related to Kraft’s new identity and whereabouts are still not declassified by Britain or US to this day.

posts.title: Battleship Potemkin not given Censor Certificate
posts.excerpt: A news in today’s TOI (17th Dec, 2025) reports that few films scheduled to be screened have landed in trouble at the 30th Thiruvananthapuram International Film Festival. Censor Board has not granted these films exemption certificates for screening. This list includes 3 films from the Palestine Package and a very high-profile film Battleship Potemkin. Whatever […]
posts.content:
A news in today’s TOI (17th Dec, 2025) reports that few films scheduled to be screened have landed in trouble at the 30th Thiruvananthapuram International Film Festival. Censor Board has not granted these films exemption certificates for screening. This list includes 3 films from the Palestine Package and a very high-profile film Battleship Potemkin. Whatever the politics behind censorship exemptions but I couldn’t help share at least the long history behind the incident of the Battleship Potemkin.

It all starts with the Russian defeat at the hands of Japan in 1905 (Russo-Japanese War over control of Manchuria) sent shockwaves across the globe. For the first time in modern history, an Asian power had decisively defeated a major European empire thus shattering the long-held myth of Western racial and military invincibility.

Revolutionaries like Aurobindo Ghosh, Bipin Chandra Pal, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai and later Rash Behari Bose and the Anushilan Samiti drew direct inspiration from Russia’s defeat in 1905. Japan’s victory did not just motivate resistance, it convinced Indian revolutionaries that armed struggle against a European empire was not only possible, but historically inevitable.   

On the other hand, Russia’s humiliation in 1905 exposed the fragility of the Tsarist state, triggering mass strikes, peasant uprisings, and mutinies across the empire. The most dramatic symbol of this internal collapse came in June 1905, when sailors aboard the Battleship Potemkin in the Black Sea, rebelled against their officers and shot their senior commanders point blank.

Soviet filmmaker Sergei Eisenstein immortalised this naval mutiny in his 1925 cult film Battleship Potemkin a silent master piece. Since then, this movie has been taught across the world including India in “all” film schools and have been inspiration for generations of film-makers.

2025 celebrates the centenary year of Battleship Potemkin and have been screened across the world with the final screening being planned for Thiruvananthapuram Film Fest in Dec. Hence withholding Censor Certification for this film simply trumps the imagination.

However, if anyone is interested to watch this masterpiece then head to Youtube for a free show: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a_bkBbrdyyw

posts.title: Vijay Diwas & Creation of Bangladesh
posts.excerpt: 54 years back, on 16th Dec 1971, at 16:31 hours, Lt. Gen. A.A.K. Niazi of Pakistan signed the Instrument of Surrender before Lt. Gen. Jagjit Singh Aurora in Dhaka.As 93,000 Pakistani troops laid down arms ending one of 20th centuries’ worst genocides, India birthed a new nation in South Asia ~ Bangladesh. This was an […]
posts.content:
54 years back, on 16th Dec 1971, at 16:31 hours, Lt. Gen. A.A.K. Niazi of Pakistan signed the Instrument of Surrender before Lt. Gen. Jagjit Singh Aurora in Dhaka.
As 93,000 Pakistani troops laid down arms ending one of 20th centuries’ worst genocides, India birthed a new nation in South Asia ~ Bangladesh.

This was an almost impossible task against U.S. backed, Chinese-supported military regime of Pakistan. There have been demands that Indira Gandhi should have negotiated Kashmir issue in return for these 93,000 Pakistani troops, but these demands do not consider that Bangladesh was birthed against overwhelming odds.

Also, Bangladesh with its geographic location, international land & maritime borders and 10 times the population of united Kashmir called for more strategic challenges needed for nation building from GOI.  

Indian Government have always been very careful and muted in its celebration of #Vijay_Diwas, to give space for Bangladeshi Nationalism through the narrative of Mukti-Juddo and Mukti-Bahini.

But 54 years on, Bangladesh has again become destabilised & volatile under Pakistani ISI and Saudi extremist influence. A section of Bangladesh has become a part of the anti-India radical Islamic axis and threatens the sovereignty of India and minority lives of its nation state.

History reminds us of a deeper truth ~ there are no permanent victories, only permanent interests. Nevertheless, today on 16th Dec, India celebrates its biggest and undoubtedly grandest political-military victory since its independence.

#Vijay_Diwas #Jai_Hind

posts.title: The Dash to Dhaka ~ Indias War with Pakistan
posts.excerpt: 11th December 1971, 54 years ago to this day, the destiny of South Asia changed forever. India and Pakistan were locked in a high-velocity, all-out war. India’s original plan was not to capture Dhaka. The military aim was limited ~ liberate major districts, secure territory for the government-in-exile of Bangladesh, and avoid provoking superpower intervention. […]
posts.content:
11th December 1971, 54 years ago to this day, the destiny of South Asia changed forever. India and Pakistan were locked in a high-velocity, all-out war. India’s original plan was not to capture Dhaka. The military aim was limited ~ liberate major districts, secure territory for the government-in-exile of Bangladesh, and avoid provoking superpower intervention.

But the war moved faster than anyone predicted.

The fall of multiple garrisons ~ Jessore on 6 Dec, Mymensingh on 7 Dec, Brahmanbaria on 7–8 Dec & Sylhet para-drop on 7 Dec. This forced Gen. Sam Manekshaw to reconsider the entire campaign. On 8 December, Lt. Gen. Jagjit Singh Aurora from Calcutta issued the now-legendary directive, “Converge on Dhaka.”

This triggered one of the largest and fastest troop movements in Indian military history “The Dash to Dhaka”. This was a three-axis bypass and convergence unseen since the Second World War.

On 11th December, the war entered its geopolitical climax. U.S. President Richard Nixon deployed the nuclear-powered carrier USS Enterprise with Task Force 74 to the Bay of Bengal. Washington wanted to “scare India and save Pakistan.” The U.S. feared India could break Pakistan into “three pieces,” undermine America’s ally Iran (this was before the 1979 Revolution), and stop the tilt of Asian balance towards the Soviet Union.

Moscow reacted within hours. Two nuclear-armed Soviet cruisers and a submarine group began shadowing the USS Enterprise. Brezhnev personally assured Indira Gandhi of unwavering support. The message sent to Washington through diplomatic backchannels was blunt, “any unilateral intervention will be met with force.”

The Soviet umbrella was now fully open.

Russia vetoed three U.S.-backed ceasefire resolutions between 4–13 December and kept China neutral by massing troops across the Sino-Soviet frontier.

In Dhaka, Lt. Gen. A.A.K. Niazi sent desperate signals to Rawalpindi (Pakistan Army GHQ) “Dhaka is militarily indefensible.”

The next 5 days saw history unfold – militarily, diplomaticaly and most importantly the ethos of being a human was restored as the genocide of 30 lakh bengalis by “khan sena” was stopped. But by then over 1.2 crore bengalis mostly hindus have moved over to India. It was the second mass exodus after the partition crisis just 2 decades back.

On 16th December 1971, Bangladesh was born, and the largest military surrender of 93000 pakistani soldiers since World War II took place in Dhaka.

If you are fascinated like me about the events shaping our immediate neighbourhood and India’s greatest battle with our primary adversary, then check out “India’s Wars” by Arjun Subramaniam – Air Vice Marshall and Senior Faculty at National Defence College.

hashtag#vijay_diwas

posts.title: The Fascinating Story of War & Finance
posts.excerpt: Akshat Shrivatsav’s post on 5th Dec “Why is INR falling?” reminded me of the background story of “Reparations-Debts Triangle” of the 1920’s which led to the Great Depression and eventually to the Global Financial crisis. This is a fascinating story of international finance and geo-political skullduggery. Read on … At the end of World War […]
posts.content:
Akshat Shrivatsav’s post on 5th Dec “Why is INR falling?” reminded me of the background story of “Reparations-Debts Triangle” of the 1920’s which led to the Great Depression and eventually to the Global Financial crisis. This is a fascinating story of international finance and geo-political skullduggery. Read on …

At the end of World War 1, the victors were Britain France and America. They took extremely harsh measures against the losers of the war – the two great powers Ottoman Empire and the Hapsburg Empire were broken up into 20 small nation states. While Germany lost crucial territories but the most humiliating part was when Britain & France asked for reparations of 132 billion gold marks – a staggering amount which broke the German economy. This impossible demand created what economic historians call the “reparations–debts triangle” :-

  1. Germany paid reparations to Britain and France.
  2. Britain and France used that money to repay their war debts to the US.
  3. The US then lent money back to Germany, mainly through private American banks.

As American banks profited massively from lending to the Germans they invested their profits in US stock market. Now since America was the supplier of finished products – specially arms & ammunitions to Europe during war time, American manufacturing also boomed and people were flushed with money which again got invested in stock market.

As the stock prices soared, retail and institutional investors alike started borrowing more and more from the banks to invest, which created an unprecedented bubble. This gave rise to the American decade of “roaring 20’s” which saw mad scramble speculative stock purchases with borrowed money. Contrasting scenes were playing out in Germany where hyper-inflation caused the economy to succumb to economic destitution. 

In 1929 as The U.S. Federal Reserve raised interest rates to stop reckless speculation, it made borrowing more expensive, especially for “stock market speculators” and “German banks all of whom relied on U.S. loans”. 2 scenarios played out ~ German banks could not borrow at this higher interest rate and influential financiers in America started selling large volumes of stock to book profit. This spooked the smaller investors, and this fear gave rise to Selling → Falling prices → More fear → More selling and confidence evaporated completely. Banks suffered massive losses and collapsed. This ended the “Reparation-Debts Triangle”.

As a result, U.S. banks stopped lending –> Germany could not pay reparations –> Britain and France could not repay war debts to US –> World trade collapsed causing the Great Depression. From this rose the Bretton Woods system and within a decade dollar became the global anchor currency.

Decades later now the financial pundits are predicting cracks in the dollar hegemony and a possibility of return to an earlier gold system amidst the steady erosion of Rupee value and rising stock & bullion markets.

While writing this article I could not help noticing that Vladimir Putin’s visit to India has resulted in interesting joint statements ~ “Russia and India have agreed to continue jointly developing systems of bilateral settlements through use of the national currencies including settlements through central bank digital currency platforms.” This comes at a time when Trumps bullying/diplomacy is playing out around the world through sanctions & tariffs.

While pundit’s crystal-gaze about what lies ahead, we are definitely living through a momentous period in history. Oh, by the way, Germany made its final World War I reparation payment on 3rd October 2010, nearly 92 years after the reparation demands were made by the victorious superpowers of that time – Britain & France.

If you are interested and want to know more about the World War Financing and role of Indians in this complex geo-political story, then do check out my book on :-

posts.title: Earlier Russia-US State Visits to India & Interesting Anecdotes
posts.excerpt: There is a raging controversy that while Shashi Tharoor was invited to the state dinner hosted for Russian President Vladimir Putin, the opposition leaders read Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge were not invited. Tharoor attended the party yesterday with his usual charm and is travelling today (6.12.2025) to Bangalore (hopefully not by Indigo) to speak […]
posts.content:
There is a raging controversy that while Shashi Tharoor was invited to the state dinner hosted for Russian President Vladimir Putin, the opposition leaders read Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge were not invited. Tharoor attended the party yesterday with his usual charm and is travelling today (6.12.2025) to Bangalore (hopefully not by Indigo) to speak at the Bangalore Literature Festival.

He is scheduled to speak at 7pm as per schedule and is sure to be asked about this controversy and other anecdotes from Putin’s India visit. Before I get to hear him speak (always a fan-boy moment for me), I couldn’t help remember few other anecdotes from earlier visits of state heads. These anecdotes were recorded later by diplomats present in the meetings in their books, memoirs or interviews.

Leonid Brezhnev’s Visit to India (December 1980)

Context: Indira Gandhi had just returned to power (Jan 1980). The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (Dec 1979) had triggered global backlash. India was under pressure from the West to condemn Moscow.

Anecdote 1: The Afghanistan conversation that India recorded internally

Brezhnev privately pressed Indira Gandhi for a favourable public statement on the Soviet war in Afghanistan. Indian officials note that Gandhi refused point-blank, arguing “This region cannot handle another decade of great-power experiments.” But she also refused to condemn Moscow outright, a delicate balancing act that kept Indo-Soviet ties intact while signalling discomfort.

Anecdote 2: Brezhnev’s gift that shaped India’s defence posture

The visit produced the 1980 Indo-Soviet Long-Term Programme for Military Cooperation — the framework that eventually enabled India to license-produce T-72 tanks and MIG-27s. This single visit influenced India’s defence structure for decades.

Amit Das Gupta in his book Moscow and Delhi: Partners in the Cold War? Records Brezhnev told Indira Gandhi “The world situation is changing rapidly. Stability in Asia requires stronger cooperation between our two countries. India must have the defence capacity to withstand pressures from any direction.”

Indira Gandhi’s responded “India cannot become dependent on any one power, even a friendly one. But we must strengthen our security, especially in our neighbourhood. We need regular, assured supplies and co-production, not one-time purchases.”

She made two demands:

  1. Technology transfer, not just supply
  2. Local assembly/manufacturing of Soviet systems to reduce vulnerability during crises

These points formed the core of the negotiation.

The second series of anecdotes present a diametrically opposite view of the India-US relations. The following excerpts from one of my favourite book of geo-politics ~ Gary J Bass’es book the Blood Telegram. Gary was the ambassador to East Pakistan based out of Dhaka in 1971 when India broke Pakistan into two, birthing Bangladesh after the genocide of Bengalis by Pakistan’s army or khan sena as is popularly remembered.

2. Richard Nixon’s Secretive & Tense Visit to India (1969)

Context: Nixon deeply disliked Indians, especially Indira Gandhi, as revealed in the declassified White House tapes. These tapes reveal that Nixon repeated referred to Indira Gandhi as “that Bitch” while speaking to Henry Kissinger. Kissinger was the US National Security Advisor in 1969 and later became Secretary of State.

Anecdote 1 — Nixon wanted the visit “cut short”

Before arriving, Nixon told Henry Kissinger “Let’s get this India thing over with as quickly as possible.” He wanted a symbolic appearance before flying to meet Pakistan’s military dictator Yahya Khan, whom he adored. Yahya Khan has just come to power in a military coup removing his predecessor, Ayub Khan. Now lets not complicate the claims that Yayha Khan’s coming to power was a covert CIA regime change project to influence South Asian politics.

Anecdote 2 — Indira Gandhi’s silence that rattled Nixon

During their meeting, Indira Gandhi responded to several of Nixon’s Pakistan-tilted answers with long pauses “The Prime Minister’s silences appeared to unnerve the President.” Nixon later told Kissinger and his other aides “That woman… she gives you nothing.” Yet Indian diplomats recalled that her silence was strategic, forcing Nixon to over-explain his position.

Anecdote 3 — The moment Nixon realised India was not intimidated

When Nixon hinted that India should “show restraint” toward Pakistan, Indira Gandhi replied calmly “Mr. President, peace is not kept by advising the victim.” This became one of the most quoted lines in Indo-US diplomatic history.

Now, whether today Tharoor addresses the guest-list furore or not, the real drama lies in India’s long history of negotiating world powers from Brezhnev’s tanks to Nixon’s tantrums. And as he speaks tonight in the Bangalore Lit Fest, one truth holds India’s diplomacy has always been larger than its dinners, and far sharper than its headlines.

Richard Nixon & Indira Gandhi

posts.title: Cold War 2.0: Sentencing In-Absentia & Syrian Fault-line
posts.excerpt: The cold war playbook of in-absentia sentencings are back. In neighbouring Bangladesh sentencing of Sheikh Hasina to death is just one amongst many similar incidences of 2025. The Democratic Republic of Congo issued a death sentence to ex-president Kabila, and Tunisia convicted President Marzouki on terrorism charges, both sentencing in-absentia and both countries now governed […]
posts.content:
The cold war playbook of in-absentia sentencings are back. In neighbouring Bangladesh sentencing of Sheikh Hasina to death is just one amongst many similar incidences of 2025.

The Democratic Republic of Congo issued a death sentence to ex-president Kabila, and Tunisia convicted President Marzouki on terrorism charges, both sentencing in-absentia and both countries now governed by administrations firmly within Washington’s sphere of influence.

On the other side Russia is playing a tit-for-tat game. A similar in-absentia sentencing have taken place in Kyrgyzstan and Central African Republic. Both countries have ruling regimes under Kremlin’s influence.

But the most dramatic symbol of this shifting order lies in Syria. For thirteen years Syria burned during which Bashar Al-Assad clung to power, which finally ended on 8 December 2024, when a rebel coalition punched through the last defensive rings around Damascus.

The scene that followed was similar to Vietnam / Afghanistan evacuation only this time it was the Russia backed dictator slipping out of his own capital before it collapsed around him. A convoy of armoured SUVs rushed him to a military airstrip at Mezzeh; a Russian jet lifted him out just hours before rebel fighters seized the presidential palace. Assad was given sanctuary in Moscow.

Now in 2025 Germany, France, Netherlands & Sweden files are being opened on Assad’s war crimes, torture, enforced disappearance, and chemical attacks. Assad is going to face a trial in-absentia and probably be sentenced to a capital punishment.

But the next twist in the plot is simply unimaginable. Ahmed Al Sharaa is an ex-jihadist field commander with links to Al-Qaeda and actively fought in the Syrian “civil” war against the US forces. Al-Sharaa is Syria’s new head of state after Assad’s fall.

Less than a year after Assad’s departure, November ’25 saw Al-Sharaa walking through the gates of the White House and shaking hands with US President Donald Trump. This is truly a masterclass in the opportunism of American foreign policy where the same US administration which had previously designated him a global terrorist is now cozying up to him.
Oh and the great MAGA boss in the White House, asked Al-Sharaa in the media interaction with a twinkle in his eyes “how many wives do you have”?

As we watch US embrace a former global jihadist while ex-heads of states face trials in-absentia, it is worth remembering that the world has seen the map of Syria redrawn a century ago during the 1st World War. It was British Indian forces who captured Damascus to Aleppo and decapitated the mighty Ottoman Empire. posts.excerpt: Out of 193 countries that are currently UN member states, Britain has invaded or fought conflicts in the territory of 171. That’s almost 90% of the planet, a geopolitical shadow stretching from the Arctic Circle to the depth of the Indian Ocean. posts.content:
Out of 193 countries that are currently UN member states, Britain has invaded or fought conflicts in the territory of 171. That’s almost 90% of the planet, a geopolitical shadow stretching from the Arctic Circle to the depth of the Indian Ocean. Its estimated that every 6 days some nation somewhere celebrates independence from British occupation. Only 22 countries escaped British invasion in the long 500 year old global history.

There aren’t many gaps on the map, but some of the more notable include Sweden, Belarus and Vatican City. The biggest blank spots can be seen on the African continent, even though the Royal African Company founded in 1660, a Crown-chartered monopoly created to control Britain’s Atlantic slave trade, shipped lakhs of enslaved Africans to the Americas for profit. This was younger by 60 years to the East India Company which was equally devastating for India and entire Asia.

The first great pushback to the British came in 1776, when the thirteen colonies declared themselves the United States of America, the first major breakaway from British rule. The next earthquake arrived in 1947, when the Indian subcontinent shattered into India, West Pakistan & East Pakistan (today’s Bangladesh). India’s independence set off a domino which cracked the imperial system itself.

Between 1947 and 1967, in just two breathless decades, more than 40 new countries were born across Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. In 1914, the world held barely 55 sovereign states, by the mid-1970s after Asia and Africa broke free there were 140+. After the Soviet collapse in 1990, the count rose past 190.

Some episodes feel like lost chapters of a global adventure saga and none more dramatic than the unravelling of Ottoman Arabia during and after World War I. What began as a desert uprising, fuelled by Indian gold, railway sabotage, and secret diplomacy, ended with an entire region being carved into 9 new states ~ Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, and the United Arab Emirates.

If you’re curious about how these transformations shaped India’s own destiny and how India aided with gold & soldiers to the formation of these Arab nations, you’ll find a deeper exploration in my book Indian Independence & World War 1.

posts.excerpt: On November 18, 2025, Sotheby’s New York witnessed history. Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer sold for a staggering $236.4 million (INR 2000 crore), becoming the highest-priced modern art ever sold.This portrait once belonged to Vienna’s elite Jewish-industrialist Lederer family who patronised Klimt and the radical vision of modern art. Their home, filled with Klimt, […]
posts.content:
On November 18, 2025, Sotheby’s New York witnessed history. Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer sold for a staggering $236.4 million (INR 2000 crore), becoming the highest-priced modern art ever sold.
This portrait once belonged to Vienna’s elite Jewish-industrialist Lederer family who patronised Klimt and the radical vision of modern art. Their home, filled with Klimt, Schiele and avant-garde aesthetics, represented the height of cosmopolitan grandeur in the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

But in 1914, the 1st World War erupted. The Habsburg monarchy, one of Europe’s oldest imperial houses disintegrated into 8 small nations – Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, etc. With this, Vienna’s elite society faced economic hardship, political turmoil and an identity crisis. Klimt’s portrait was made when the war was being raged between 1914–1916, captures Elisabeth Lederer at the twilight of the old Imperial Europe ~ graceful, adorned, unaware of the storm that would soon sweep away her entire world.
After the Nazi takeover of Austria in 1938, life changed catastrophically for Jewish families. The Lederer’s were forcibly displaced and their massive collection of extraordinary arts especially Klimt’s works were seized by the Nazis. These artworks were catalogued, stored, and dispersed across the Third Reich as part of systematic cultural plunder.

Elisabeth Lederer died in 1944 after years of persecution. Her parents have already died by this time. However, this portrait narrowly survived World War II after being separated from other Klimt works that were later destroyed in a fire at Immendorf Castle in Austria. Only her brother Erich Lederer survived in exile, later fighting a long legal battle to reclaim what was stolen. In 1948, this portrait was reinstated to him.

It is not just a masterpiece of beauty, but a symbol of injustice, resilience, and remembrance – telling the story of a family which lost everything except the memory preserved in art. If this piques your interest to know more about the Indian connection to the World War 1 then do check out my book Indian Revolution & World War 1.

P.S. At the end of the 18th century, Vienna’s royal court celebrated a musical prodigy — Mozart. But few know that his contemporary, the court painter Johann Zoffany, travelled to India and created some of the most striking and controversial artworks of the era. Legend even claims he became the only cannibal in the history of royal art. Curious? Do check out my video (https://lnkd.in/grXabuyj
) on Zoffany, an artist whose wild life and extraordinary paintings have long fascinated me.

On 12 November 2025, two days after the Delhi blast and as Indian media began reporting Turkish links to the attack, another headline erupted – a Turkish military cargo plane returning from Azerbaijan crashed in Georgia, killing all 20 onboard. (Reuters: https://lnkd.in/giEDaJEW)

These personnel had been in Baku for Azerbaijan’s Victory Day parade, celebrating its 2020 triumph over Armenia. The controversy now raging, was it a mechanical failure or a missile/drone strike?

But before we go forward, lets rewind to look at what had happened after the 2016 military coup and Erdoğan’s assassination attempt.

Erdoğan publicly accused the assassination attempt on the U.S. based cleric Fethullah Gülen. When Washington refused to extradite Gülen immediately, Erdoğan interpreted it as US & NATO complicity.

Within a month, he pivoted dramatically, meeting Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, signing a civil nuclear deal and purchasing the S-400 Triumf missile system. The same Russian system India used extensively during Operation Sindoor, making Erdoğan’s move even more shocking for the U.S. and NATO.

Politically cornered after 2016, Erdoğan transformed himself from a reformist democrat into a hard-line Islamist. He re-Islamised Turkish public life and revived Ottoman symbolism, positioning Türkiye and himself — as the defender of the global Muslim Umma (community). This ideological shift opened the door to deep military and strategic outreach with Pakistan.

Behind the scenes, Erdoğan consolidated power by building what analysts call a family-centred deep state. Key sectors ~ energy, finance, the sovereign wealth fund, defence procurement, major construction contracts, and education foundations, increasingly revolve around figures within his inner circle.

Türkiye hasn’t seen this level of concentrated power since the Young Turk era, which culminated in the Ottoman call for global jihad against Britain, France, and Russia, igniting World War I.

The Jewish holocaust is widely known, but its grim template emerged with the genocide of Armenians during World War I and to avenge it, Armenian operatives after the war hunted down the perpetrators one-by-one. Decades later, Israel echoed this strategy after 2nd World War, pursuing Nazi officers worldwide.

The most prominent effort was conducted by the Jewish group Nakam meaning avengers. 2 years after the last of the most brutal Nazi leader – Adolf Eichmann, was apprehended by Mossad, legendary Jewish-American cartoonist’s Stan Lee & Jack Kirby working for Marvel Comics created a league of superheroes ~ “The Avengers”.

From 1947 to 2015, Türkiye was generally neutral with India. However, everything changed in 2016 with a Coup in Turkish Military & assassination attempt of President Erdoğan.

On the night of 15th July 2016, tanks rolled into Turkish capital Ankara and historic city of Istanbul. Turkish F-16s bombed the parliament. Erdoğan was vacationing in the coastal resort of Marmaris. Around 10:30 p.m., Erdoğan received warnings from loyal intelligence officers and aides that a coup was underway.

The “assassination unit”, was helicoptered in from Dalaman airbase. Just as the Presidential convoy slipped out through the pine forest roads, another sound rose in the distance — the chopping rotors of helicopters cutting through the coastal air.

The assassination unit had arrived at the Marmaris hotel. The timing was diabolical. Two moving lines, two destinies, one racing from the hotel to the Dalaman Airport, the other from the Dalaman Airport to the hotel, crossing paths in the dark.

posts.title: Blood Diamonds to Civil Wars: How the Empire’s Greed Shaped the World
posts.excerpt: After 1947, Portugal stood defiant, a small nation clinging to its fading glory with 3 remaining major colonies – Goa in India, Angola & Mozambique in Africa. Under António Salazar, Portugal entered a new phase of denial — the Estado Novo, or “New State.” Salazar’s was a dictatorship built on opportunism, convinced that the Portuguese […]
posts.content:
After 1947, Portugal stood defiant, a small nation clinging to its fading glory with 3 remaining major colonies – Goa in India, Angola & Mozambique in Africa. Under António Salazar, Portugal entered a new phase of denial — the Estado Novo, or “New State.” Salazar’s was a dictatorship built on opportunism, convinced that the Portuguese Empire was not colonial but “a single, indivisible nation spread across continents.”

Meanwhile, India just freed from two centuries of British rule, was trying to stitch together the torn fabric of its geography. As protracted negotiations failed, in 1961 Indian troops marched into Goa. The Portuguese governor, after brief resistance, surrendered.

In Lisbon, Salazar refused to accept defeat — he declared that Goa was still “Portuguese territory under foreign occupation.” For thirteen years, Portuguese schoolchildren were taught that Goa would one day return to Portugal, but it never did.

Salazar died in 1970 and soon his legacy came to a close with the Carnation Revolution in Lisbon, when soldiers refused to shoot. Salazar’s regime is associated with decades of political repression and keeping Portugal as Western Europe’s most economically backward, uneducated, and poor nation.

The Portuguese military, exhausted by 13 years of counter-insurgency in Africa, simply walked away. Independence came almost overnight — but the new African nations inherited no functioning state, no unified army, no shared identity.

That sudden vacuum became the spark.

This was the height of Cold War – a global conflict between Soviet Russia with Communist ideology against the United States as the epicentre of Capitalism. Civil War started in both Angola and Mozambique where US Army, deeply racist South Africa and white ruled Zimbabwe started fighting against communist guerillas assisted by Soviet Russia & Cuban troops.

Ideology was just a smoke screen, Mozambique had major oil reserves while Angola along with Congo (DRC) and Sierre Leone has world’s major diamond reserves. These regions had little state control, making diamonds the perfect war currency: small, easy to smuggle, impossible to trace, and worth millions.

The world’s diamond supply chain controlled by De Beers, headquartered in London and Johannesburg in South Africa, depended heavily on stones from across Africa and especially these war-torn areas. The logic for local warlords was simple, whoever held the mines could buy weapons, food, and loyalty.

Dubai emerges as Diamond Trading Hub

Closer home, The city of Dubai in UAE emerged as a major diamond-trading centre and, importantly in the context of illicit trade, was identified (2000s onwards) as a key hub for smuggling “conflict minerals or blood diamonds”. Dubai’s Multi Commodities Centre and the Dubai Diamond Exchange became focal points; Dubai’s diamond throughput jumped from ~$3 million from 2001 to $35 billion by 2010 (rough + polished), as per DMCC & Reuters; by 2011, Dubai Diamond Exchange reported $39 billion being traded.

Antwerp & Diamond Smuggling

In Europe, the city of Antwerp in Belgium has a long history in the diamond trade (cutting, polishing, trading) but in the context of “conflict / blood diamonds”, it is documented that from the late 1990s and early 2000s, Antwerp was involved in high-profile smuggling cases of diamonds specially from Sierra Leone, Democratic Republic of Congo & other conflicted African countries, entering legitimate trade channels.

De Beers up for sale

In 2025 the South Africa Head Quartered De Beers under severe financial stress, competition from Lab Grown Diamonds (LGDs) and massive geo-political pressure is up for sale by its holding company Anglo American plc. The holding company has drawn interest from at least six consortia, including commodities billionaire Anil Agarwal, Indian diamond firms, Qatari investment funds, Botswana Government and Govt. of Angola.

The story of the diamond is not about beauty or brilliance — it’s about memory. Each stone is a mirror reflecting what humanity has chosen to forget — that behind every sparkle, there’s always a shadow.

However, if this story intrigued you, you’ll love exploring the deeper history of how the thousand-year-old Portuguese monarchy collapsed on the eve of World War I, which set off a domino chain of revolutions across Europe eventually triggering the World War 1.

How, just a hundred kilometres from Antwerp, the world saw its first poison-gas attack at Ypres and standing in that greenish cloud of chlorine gas, were the Indian brigades of the British Army, gasping, fighting, and dying on foreign soil. The forced conscription of Indians by the British to serve as German cannon fodder, became one of the sparks that ignited India’s underground revolutionary movement, a story largely forgotten today.

To uncover this lost chapter of global and Indian history, get your copy of Indian Revolution & World War I — and rediscover how the Great War changed the destiny of nations far beyond Europe.

posts.title: The deal that could have changed India’s map
posts.excerpt: By the dawn of the 20th century, Portugal’s monarchy was a hollow shell. The House of Braganza, one of Europe’s most ruthless and enduring dynasties, was in shambles. The Portuguese Empire, which had once stretched from Brazil to the East Indies, had withered to three scraps of territory: Angola, Mozambique, and Goa. In 1908, Portugal […]
posts.content:
By the dawn of the 20th century, Portugal’s monarchy was a hollow shell. The House of Braganza, one of Europe’s most ruthless and enduring dynasties, was in shambles. The Portuguese Empire, which had once stretched from Brazil to the East Indies, had withered to three scraps of territory: Angola, Mozambique, and Goa.

In 1908, Portugal dreamed of a comeback, an African land bridge connecting Angola and Mozambique across modern-day Zambia, Malawi, and Zimbabwe. This dream was mapped out in Lisbon as the Mapa Cor-de-Rosa, the Rose-Coloured Map.

But Britain had its own fantasy: a continuous imperial corridor from Cairo to Cape Town, stitched together by railways and telegraph lines. The man behind it was Cecil Rhodes — Prime Minister of Cape Colony, empire’s visionary, and the blood-diamond baron who built the De Beers monopoly.

He turned diamonds into symbols of eternal love — while hiding that they were paid for with broken backs, shattered skulls, and African blood.
Britain issued an ultimatum. Lisbon, weak and humiliated, backed down. Outrage followed. Portugal’s people rose against the monarchy, calling it a puppet of London.

In February 1908, as King Carlos I and Crown Prince Luís Filipe rode through Lisbon, two men from the secret anti-monarchist society Carbonária stepped forward. Shots rang out — the King was killed instantly, the Crown Prince mortally wounded. Within two years, in October 1910, the First Portuguese Republic was proclaimed, ending nearly a thousand years of Braganza rule.

By 1947, this same weakened Portugal was approached by the land-locked Princely State of Hyderabad. The Nizam sought to buy Goa, to open a gateway to the Arabian Sea and create a direct trade route to the Gulf States. Mir Nawaz Jung arrived in London as the Agent-General of Hyderabad in April 1947, discussed the Goa proposal and had a meeting with a Portuguese rep in June 1947.

Portugal refused.

Had the deal gone through, India’s map might have looked very different. Hyderabad could have become a maritime power in the heart of the subcontinent. Incidentally, the world’s most famous diamond, the Koh-i-Noor, was mined from the Golconda mines, near the Krishna-Godavari delta. Thankfully, diamond yields there were poor by the mid 20th century and the mines have went silent long back.

Because imagine if Golconda had been rich in active diamond seams in 1947 ~ amid Partition’s chaos, India might have seen a fate like Sierra Leone, Congo, or Angola – a fractured militia-ridden land, soaked in blood and greed.

History has strange what-ifs. Sometimes, it is not what we gain, but what we narrowly avoid, that shapes a nation’s destiny.

To uncover this lost chapter of global and Indian history, get your copy of Indian Revolution & World War I.

The Rose Coloured Map, which eventually led to the fall of the Portugese Monarchy

posts.title: Ocean of Civilisations
posts.excerpt: Long before the age of sail, India mastered the monsoon winds. At the end of the monsoon season, winds turn from west to east, aiding navigation across the Bay of Bengal. In the ancient time (between 5CE to 15 CE) this marked the start of the trading journey from India’s east coast – Orissa and […]
posts.content:
Long before the age of sail, India mastered the monsoon winds. At the end of the monsoon season, winds turn from west to east, aiding navigation across the Bay of Bengal. In the ancient time (between 5CE to 15 CE) this marked the start of the trading journey from India’s east coast – Orissa and Bengal to what we call today as South East Asia – Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, Philippines, Cambodia, Myanmar, Et al.

Buddhism – India’s biggest cultural export to the world also spread through this trade route. When we stand before the grand Borobudur in Java — the world’s largest Buddhist temple — we are not just seeing Indonesian craftsmanship. We are seeing the soul of Ratnagiri and Udayagiri from coastal Odisha, whose terraced stupas and mandala plans – concentric squares leading to the cosmic axis — symbolizing step by step spiritual ascent. The structure is adorned with thousands of carved relief panels depicting Buddhist stories and teachings from the Jataka tales.

And when the morning sun lights up the lotus towers of Angkor Wat world’s largest Hindu Temple (ironically it’s not in India), its spires rise in a rhythm hauntingly similar to the shikhara of Konark Sun Temple and Puri’s Jagannath Temple, both employ axial alignment with solar pathways, intricate narrative reliefs, and maritime motifs—testifying to shared cosmological ideas transmitted via this maritime channel. In Cambodia, Khmer inscriptions mention merchants and Brahmins from Kalinga and Gauda, who contributed to temple rituals and construction ideologies.

Today on Karthik Purnima (5th Nov 2025), this Millenium old cultural link, will be remembered and commemorated across the eastern coast of India – where people will perform puja and float miniature boats made of paper, banana bark, or cork, decorated with betel leaves, lamps, and flowers, symbolizing the voyages of their ancestors. This is a living memory of India’s eastern seafaring past, a symbolic tribute to the spirit of exploration, trade, and cultural exchange that once connected India to the vast maritime world of the Indian Ocean.

Stepped Buddhist Temple of Borobudur, Indonesia

posts.excerpt: Every great maritime story begins with waves — and this one begins with silence. posts.content:
Time to Read :

Every great maritime story begins with waves — and this one begins with silence. As India Maritime Week 2025 unfurls under the proud banner of “Uniting Oceans, One Maritime Vision,” the map of India’s partner states glows bright — Gujarat, Maharashtra, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Assam, Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh.

But one coastline stays dark.
West Bengal — the state that literally gave India its window to the East and gateway to the North-East — is nowhere on the list.

Kolkata’s docks once echoed with the clang of hammers from Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers Ltd (GRSE) — a yard older than independent India, crafting warships, patrol boats, and merchant vessels that sailed under the tricolour.

From the Hooghly’s muddy edges, engineers and artisans built India’s first indigenous naval ships. The same river that carried opium and jute to the world in the 19th century today carries container freight that still ranks 5th among India’s major ports in tonnage handled — ahead of many “partner” states.

The Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata, India’s only riverine major port, quietly moves over 65 million metric tonnes of cargo each year, linking inland waterways, eastern coalfields, and northeast logistics routes.
This is not a forgotten backwater — it is the living bloodstream of India’s eastern trade.

So why is West Bengal missing from the grand maritime vision worth ₹2.20 lakh crore? How can a national blueprint for the ocean forget the land that has built ships for the navy, hosted one of the oldest dockyards, and still stands as India’s eastern maritime pivot?

It’s even more puzzling because the Union Minister of Ports, Shipping & Waterways — Shri Shantanu Thakur — hails from West Bengal. What an Irony !
